title: It Was Never Marijuana: How a Word Became a Weapon | The Bridge
h1: It Was Never "Marijuana": How a Word Became a Weapon
description: From 1937 tax stamps to New York's 2021 law: how one word got attached to fear of immigrants, and where the popular story goes too far.
lede: Before it was a national panic it was a line on a pharmacy shelf. The record of how the name changed is ugly enough without the legends.
html:
In 1937 the federal government needed tax stamps for a plant it wanted gone. It didn't bother designing any. According to the chief curator of philately at the Smithsonian's National Postal Museum, officials took stamps they had in excess, picturing long forgotten treasury secretaries, and overprinted them with one word: marihuana. The stamps weren't meant to raise money. They were meant to restrict use.

That word is the story. Our Facts page says it straight: we use cannabis, because that's what it is. Here's the record behind that choice, including the parts the popular version gets wrong.

Two drugs in the newspapers

Throughout the 19th century, American news reports and medical journals almost always used the formal name, cannabis. In the late 1800s it was a popular ingredient in medicinal products, sold openly in pharmacies. After 1900 the papers tell a different story under a different name. NPR's Code Switch quotes a 1925 New York Times headline: "Mexican, Crazed by Marihuana, Runs Amuck With Butcher Knife." It's almost, NPR noted, as though the press was describing two different drugs.

Immigration set the stage. After the Mexican Revolution of 1910, PBS Frontline's timeline records, fear and prejudice about Spanish-speaking newcomers became attached to the plant. New York's own regulator now writes that the word was historically used in a derogatory way toward certain ethnic groups, and that this is why the state says cannabis.

Where the popular story goes too far

Straight facts cut both ways. The word itself wasn't cooked up in Washington. It's Mexican Spanish, and NPR reports nobody knows for sure how it was coined, with competing theories pointing to three continents. Mexico banned the plant in 1920, 17 years before U.S. federal law. And a 2026 paper in the journal Addiction takes apart some favorite legends. It argues that Harry Anslinger played a far smaller part in passing the Act than popular histories claim, that he first opposed federal prohibition for practical reasons, that he refused to endorse Reefer Madness, and that the Act never banned hemp for fiber. So the DuPont conspiracy can rest.

What the record still shows

You don't need the legends. Anslinger, who headed the federal narcotics bureau from 1930 to 1962, told Congress the plant caused "insanity, criminality and death," and drew on what became known as his gore file. The hearing record, NPR found, included a letter from a Colorado newspaper editor about "one of our degenerate Spanish-speaking residents." By Ohio State's account, the House passed the bill after less than half an hour of debate, with the Speaker explaining it was "a narcotic of some kind." The only witness who spoke against it was from the American Medical Association, and congressmen accused that witness of obstructionism.

New York pushed back early. In 1944 Mayor Fiorello La Guardia and the New York Academy of Medicine produced a report calling marijuana a mild intoxicant, and an article solicited by Anslinger attacked it in advance. In 1969, in Leary v. United States, the Supreme Court threw out a conviction under the Act on self-incrimination grounds. A year later Congress put the plant in the most restrictive drug category there is.

The word in 2021

New York's 2021 law still carries the old spelling in its name, the Marihuana Regulation and Taxation Act. Read its statement of intent and you get this: "to regulate, control, and tax marihuana, heretofore known as cannabis." Backwards, if you know the history. But the same section says existing laws "have disproportionately impacted African-American and Latinx communities," and the Cannabis Law that came out of it uses cannabis throughout.

A word never arrested anybody. People did that, with a vocabulary that made it easier. We say cannabis. The science didn't change. The language did.
